content: Syntex Laboratorios Syntex SA was a pharmaceutical company established in Mexico City in 1944 by Russell Marker. The company specialized in the production of therapeutic steroids derived from the Mexican yam. In 1994, Syntex became part of the Roche group. Russell Marker, the founder of Syntex, left the company after a dispute over compensation and took his research notebooks with him. George Rosenkranz, who had studied at the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology and was conducting pharmaceutical research in Cuba, joined Syntex to replace Marker. Rosenkranz subsequently hired Carl Djerassi. Carl Djerassi began working at Syntex in 1949 as the associate director of chemical research. Under his leadership, the team achieved the first synthesis of norethindrone, the first orally active progestin. This breakthrough was instrumental in the development of some of the earliest oral contraceptives. Luis E. Miramontes joined Syntex in 1950 as a researcher under Djerassi's supervision, after moving from the National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM). On October 15, 1951, Miramontes successfully performed the first synthesis of an orally active progestin. The compound, 19-nor-17α-ethynyltestosterone, was later given the generic name norethisterone or norethindrone. This discovery also contributed to the development of early oral contraceptives. Syntex submitted their compound for biological evaluation to a laboratory in Madison, Wisconsin, and it was found to be the most active and orally effective progestational hormone of its time. In November 1951, Syntex filed a patent application for the compound. However, in August 1953, D. Searle & Co. filed a patent for the synthesis of a double-bond isomer of norethindrone, called norethynodrel. Norethynodrel converts into norethindrone under acidic conditions, but Searle's patent did not infringe on Syntex's intellectual property. Searle obtained approval to market norethynodrel before Syntex received approval for their compound. By 1964, three companies, including Syntex, were marketing 2 mg doses of Syntex's norethindrone. Additionally, Syntex chemists developed a method to synthesize cortisone from diosgenin, a phytosteroid found in Mexican yams. This process was more cost-effective than the previous synthesis method developed by Merck & Co.
